Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
In article <76vu7b$i1q$1...@nnrp1.dejanews.com>,

vte...@wizards.com (LSJ) wrote:
> jt...@cornell.edu (Joshua Duffin) wrote:
> > (it seems clear, by the way, that non-damage effects of a strike will never
> > usefully apply to the current strike phase (unless First Strike is involved,
> > of course), since strikes always resolve simultaneously.)
>
> Except for the few Thaumaturgy strikes that make the opponent's
> weapon strikes do no damage: Blood Fury, Blood Rage, Soul Burn.

Right. (Although the most recent ruling I see on a quick check of
Soul Burn says that it *doesn't* work on the current opposing strike.)
So now I have to ask: Why *do* those ones work? My guess is that their
non-damage effect ('If victim attempts to strike with a weapon this round,
victim does no damage'), while applied simultaneously with an opposing
weapon strike, ends up taking effect before damage is *resolved*, and
so the weapon strike results in no damage.

If that's the proper explanation, though, I'm not sure why Soul Burn
wouldn't also work on the current opposing strike. ('For the remainder
of this round, the opposing minion cannot inflict damage with weapons.')
The remainder of the round should include the current damage resolution
step, which does follow the strike resolution I think.

Or maybe I'm just off-base in my understanding of how non-damage effects
work and strikes resolve.

Josh

I guess I'm not clear on why Blood Rage/Fury takes effect during the
current strike resolution, but Soul Burn doesn't - even with the wording
difference. If the Rage/Fury effect is part of the strike's effect,
isn't it implemented at the same time as Soul Burn's effect would be?
And if so, why doesn't 'remainder of the round' include 'the damage
resolution step that comes right after this strike resolves'? I looked
at the original Soul Burn response, but it doesn't seem to elaborate
on the definition of 'remainder of the round'.

I can see how Dodge cancels an opposing strike's effect since (1) that's
the rulebook definition of Dodge and (2) Dodge resolves before other
strikes. But it's not obvious to me why Blood Fury/Rage should be
interpreted to have a 'cancellation' rather than Bonecraft-like effect,
except due to the timing of damage resolution vs other effects of resolving
strikes.

Josh

Joshua wrote:
> I'm not quite sure what you're saying here, Noal. The ruling you cite

For example, if Anvil and Gideon are in a combat and Gideon is the acting
minion. Anvil has a Zip Gun and Gideon has an Assault Rifle.

Gideon declares his strike to be the Assault Rifle.
Anvil declares his strike to be Blood Fury and uses Blur to strike twice with
the Zip Gun.

The Blood Fury will prevent the damage from the Assault Rifle, but not from
the Zip Gun. I don't see why Soul Burn can't be used interchangeably with
Blood Fury in this case.

> "If the opposing minion's strike is a weapon strike, that strike is unaffected
> by the Soul Burn, since Soul Burn only affects the "remainder" of this round.
> [LSJ 980213] "

from the Errata page:

Soul Burn doesn't protect the target from taking damage from a weapon

strike, since "inflict" has been ruled to mean "inflict on the opposing
minion/retainer". So side-effect damage from a Bomb, Zip Gun, etc. is

unaffected by Soul Burn. [LSJ 980216]

I see your quote on the Clarifications page. Personally, the one you quote
from the Clarifications page looks like a huge error on LSJ's part since
strike resolution is after strike declaration, which is when that clause
would take effect, IMO. I think it would be pretty idiotic to have to use
Soul Burn as a First Strike to get that clause to kick in. After all, the
card costs 1 blood and only does 1R-2R damage. Hardly worth it when you
consider Theft of Vitae, which removes 1-2 blood at range and costs nothing.

I have to agree with you on this one Josh. Sould Burn should work _exactly_
like Blood Rage and Blood Fury in this regard since that was the obvious
intent. I'm just glad that MJL tournaments aren't burdened by nonsense like
this and that we use common sense and consistency when making rulings. But
then, if WotC would hire someone that can read and write at higher than a
grade school level to edit the cards' text before printing them, we wouldn't
have this problem.

> > > non-damage effect ('If victim attempts to strike with a weapon this round,

> > > weapon strike, ends up taking effect before damage is *resolved*, and
> > > so the weapon strike results in no damage.
> >
> > VTES template: "If the opposing vampire attempts to strike with a weapon
this
> > round, he or she does no damage." Not that anything really changes there.
> >
> > Your explanation is good enough. The strike (Blood Rage/Fury) cancels
> > the opposing weapon strike's damage just as a Dodge cancels the opposing
> > strike's effect on the dodger.
>
> I guess I'm not clear on why Blood Rage/Fury takes effect during the
> current strike resolution, but Soul Burn doesn't - even with the wording
> difference. If the Rage/Fury effect is part of the strike's effect,
> isn't it implemented at the same time as Soul Burn's effect would be?

Card text on Blood Rage/Fury applies to all weapon strikes for the
round. Card text on Soul Burn applies only to the remainder of the
round.

> And if so, why doesn't 'remainder of the round' include 'the damage
> resolution step that comes right after this strike resolves'?

Even if it did, it wouldn't change the damage resolving at that time.

The weapon does some damage. Then the damage resolves.

Together with Soul Burn:

* The weapon does damage. And, for the remainder of the round, the weapon
will do no damage. And Soul Burn does 1 (or two) damage.
* The damage (from the weapon and from Soul Burn) is resolved.

> I can see how Dodge cancels an opposing strike's effect since (1) that's
> the rulebook definition of Dodge and (2) Dodge resolves before other
> strikes.

No matter when Dodge resolves, it would protect the dodging minion from the
opposing strike - that's the way the rules read. It has to resolve, though
(which is why it doesn't protect from Catatonic Fear's damage - the dodge
never resolves).

So many people are confused by that that it is typically explained that
Dodge resolves first. But that isn't important, and it isn't described
that way in the rules.

Blood Fury/Rage work somewhat like Dodge does - thwarting the current
strike by the opposing weapon - because card text says they do.

> But it's not obvious to me why Blood Fury/Rage should be
> interpreted to have a 'cancellation' rather than Bonecraft-like effect,
> except due to the timing of damage resolution vs other effects of resolving
> strikes.

Bonecraft's template is different. It doesn't affect strikes directly (by
cancelling damage, for instance) - it changes the minion's strength. And
it has (parenthetical) card text explicitly *not* affecting the current
opposing strike.

In article <7731lt$b1d$1...@nnrp1.dejanews.com>,

vte...@wizards.com (LSJ) wrote:
> jt...@cornell.edu (Joshua Duffin) wrote:
> > I guess I'm not clear on why Blood Rage/Fury takes effect during the
> > current strike resolution, but Soul Burn doesn't - even with the wording
> > difference. If the Rage/Fury effect is part of the strike's effect,
> > isn't it implemented at the same time as Soul Burn's effect would be?
>
> Card text on Blood Rage/Fury applies to all weapon strikes for the
> round. Card text on Soul Burn applies only to the remainder of the
> round.

Okay. So your reading is that 'remainder of the round' on Soul Burn
means 'the rest of the round after this strike resolution', whereas
'this round' on Blood Fury/Rage means 'this round including this
strike resolution'?

> > And if so, why doesn't 'remainder of the round' include 'the damage
> > resolution step that comes right after this strike resolves'?
>
> Even if it did, it wouldn't change the damage resolving at that time.
>
> The weapon does some damage. Then the damage resolves.
>
> Together with Soul Burn:
>
> * The weapon does damage. And, for the remainder of the round, the weapon
> will do no damage. And Soul Burn does 1 (or two) damage.
> * The damage (from the weapon and from Soul Burn) is resolved.

To my mind, the 'for the remainder of the round the weapon will do no
damage' part would work exactly like 'for this round the weapon will
do no damage' on Blood Fury - Blood Fury doesn't use the term 'cancel'
any more than Soul Burn does.

> > I can see how Dodge cancels an opposing strike's effect since (1) that's
> > the rulebook definition of Dodge and (2) Dodge resolves before other
> > strikes.
>
> No matter when Dodge resolves, it would protect the dodging minion from the
> opposing strike - that's the way the rules read. It has to resolve, though
> (which is why it doesn't protect from Catatonic Fear's damage - the dodge
> never resolves).
>
> So many people are confused by that that it is typically explained that
> Dodge resolves first. But that isn't important, and it isn't described
> that way in the rules.

Hmmm. It's not important if your definition of 'cancel' would allow it
to retroactively protect the Dodging minion. But if Dodge didn't resolve
before First Strike, it seems logical to me that a First Strike hit would
successfully do damage to a Dodging minion, since the Dodge tries to cancel
it but can't since the damage has already resolved.

> Blood Fury/Rage work somewhat like Dodge does - thwarting the current
> strike by the opposing weapon - because card text says they do.

To me, the card text doesn't make it obvious that they work by 'cancelling'
opposing weapon damage.

> > But it's not obvious to me why Blood Fury/Rage should be
> > interpreted to have a 'cancellation' rather than Bonecraft-like effect,
> > except due to the timing of damage resolution vs other effects of resolving
> > strikes.
>
> Bonecraft's template is different. It doesn't affect strikes directly (by
> cancelling damage, for instance) - it changes the minion's strength. And
> it has (parenthetical) card text explicitly *not* affecting the current
> opposing strike.

As far as I can see, Blood Fury/Rage don't affect strikes directly either.
Their 'victim's weapons do no damage this round' effect is something
applied to the opposing minion, not to the opposing strike. To my mind,
the only thing that causes Blood Fury/Rage to *effectively* cancel damage
from an opposing weapon strike is that their anti-weapon effect kicks in
before the weapon damage is actually resolved. Which could be the same
for Soul Burn, even with the different wording, since it looks to me like
timing is what makes Blood Fury/Rage work, and the timing is the same for
Blood Fury as for Soul Burn. (The difference would be if the 'remainder of
the round' text is meant specifically to exclude this current strike
resolution.)

Josh

> specifically states to place the card on the minion... the fact that it's a
strike
> just tells you when to play it, you dodge the damage but still get the card
> put on you...

Actually, this ruling is pretty much the same as the Bonecraft rules. If
you Dodge a Bonecraft hit, you will not suffer the -1/-2 hand damage
effects - Dodge negates all effects of the opposing strike on the Dodging
minion and any non-retainer cards on him/her.

You're probably thinking of what happens if Camille Devereux prevents the
damage from Bonecraft, eg with Skin of Rock: In that case, the -1/-2 hand
damage effect still happens, because preventing the damage doesn't do
anything about the other effects of the strike.

(This is also the same as Blood Fury/Blood Rage. If Joaquina Amaya prevents
the damage from Blood Rage with Apparition, she will still do no damage with
weapon strikes this round.)

Josh

Messages.Author: agen...@my-dejanews.com
Messages.Body:
>I guess that this ruling differs from the bonecraft ruling because
>bonecraft specifically states to place the card on the minion... the
>fact that it's a strike just tells you when to play it, you dodge the
>damage but still get the card put on you...

Wrong.
A Dodge cancels the opponents strike and all of it's side effects.
So if Bonecraft is dodged, then the only place that it goes is to
the ashheap.
However, if the damage from Bonecraft is prevented, then the side
effect (the -1 whatever) is still applied, since the strike was
not cancelled.
